competition: St. Petersburg Mathematical Olympiad, grade 10 (city round and selection round)

problems.problem: Two distinct quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with leading coefficients equal to one are given. It is known that $f(19)+f(92)=g(19)+g(92)$. For which $x$ does the equality $f(x)=g(x)$ hold?
Inside a unit square with marked vertices one more point is marked. Prove that there are three marked points forming a triangle of area at most $1/8$.

A digit is written on each of $N\geqslant 3$ cards. Arranging these cards in a row in all possible ways, we obtain $N!=1\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot\ldots\cdot(N-1)N$ natural numbers. Can their product be a number whose decimal representation consists of ones only?

A circle inscribed in an angle with vertex $O$ touches its sides at points $A$ and $B$. A ray $OX$ meets this circle at two points $C$ and $D$ such that $OC=CD=1$. If $M$ is the intersection point of the ray $OX$ and the segment $AB$, what is the length of the segment $OM$?

There are $1992$ stones in a pile. Two players play the following game: in a move each of them may take from the pile any number of stones that is a divisor of the number of stones taken by the opponent in his previous move. The first player may take any number of stones in his first move, but not all at once. The player who takes the last stone wins. Who wins with correct play?

A regular $n$-gon with centre $O$ is given in the plane. Denote by $\vec v_1, \vec v_2, \ldots, \vec v_n$ the vectors leading from $O$ to the vertices of the polygon, numbered in order starting from some vertex. Prove that if $a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_n$ are some real numbers, then the vector $a_1\vec v_1+a_2\vec v_2+\ldots+a_n\vec v_n$ is non-zero.

In a platoon of the national guard there serve sergeants and privates, and each private is subordinate to one or two sergeants. Prove that one can discharge into the reserve at most half of the platoon so that every remaining private is commanded by exactly one sergeant.

A point $D$ is taken inside the side $BC$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$. The line passing through the point $C$ parallel to $AD$ meets the line $AB$ at a point $E$. Prove that $CE/CD\geqslant 2\sqrt3$.
Every second $54$ or $77$ is added to a natural number. Prove that after some time a number whose last two digits coincide will be obtained.

There are $nk$ stones, distributed somehow into $n$ piles. One may double any pile by moving into it, arbitrarily, stones from the other piles. For which $k$ can one always (for every $n$) achieve by such operations that all remaining piles contain equally many stones?
Prove that if a natural number $a$ is not a perfect square, then there is a natural number $n$ such that $a=[n+\sqrt n+1/2]$.
A regular $n$-gon $M$ was rotated about its centre through the angle $\pi/n$, giving an $n$-gon $M'$. Into what smallest number of convex polygons can the figure $M\cup M'$ be cut?
The sequence $(F_n)$ is defined as follows: $F_1=1$, $F_2=2$, $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$ for every $n>0$. Prove that for every natural $n$ the inequality $$\sqrt[n]{F_{n+1}}>1+1\big/\sqrt[n]{F_n}$$ holds.

The plane is coloured in $1992$ colours, and a triangle $T$ is given in it. Prove that there is a triangle in the plane congruent to $T$ such that on each pair of its sides there are interior points of the same colour.

$128$ ones are written on the board. In one move one may replace a pair of numbers $a$ and $b$ by the number $ab+1$. Let $A$ be the largest number that can be obtained on the board after $127$ such operations. What is its last digit?
Polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are such that for every real $x$ the equality $P(x^2-x+1)=Q(x^2+x+1)$ holds. Prove that both polynomials are constants.

Inside a triangle $ABC$ lies a circle that touches its sides $AB$ and $BC$ and also passes through the point $P$, the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$. Another circle is drawn through the points $A$, $P$ and $C$. Prove that these circles are tangent to each other.

Several people divide an inheritance they have received. Call an heir "poor" if he received less than $99$ roubles in the division, and "rich" if he received more than $10$ thousand roubles. It is known that in every division of the inheritance the amount of money of the "rich" heirs is not less than that of the "poor" ones. Prove that in every division of the inheritance the amount of money of the "rich" heirs is at least $100$ times that of the "poor" heirs.

Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $\dfrac{ab}{a-b}=c$. It is also known that the numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ have no common natural divisor greater than $1$. Prove that $a-b$ is a perfect square.

A point $M$ lies inside a diameter $AB$ of a circle $S$ and is not the centre of the circle. On one side of the diameter $AB$, arbitrary distinct points $P$ and $Q$ are taken on the circle such that the segments $PM$ and $QM$ form equal angles with the diameter. Prove that all lines $PQ$ pass through one point.

In a $17\times 17$ square table, $80$ cells are painted black, and the rest are white. One may paint a row or a column black if the majority of cells on this line are black. Prove that by such operations one cannot make the whole table black.

On the set $M$ of natural numbers from $1$ to $1993$ an operation $*$ is defined which assigns to every two numbers $a$ and $b$ of the set $M$ some number $a*b$ also belonging to $M$. It is known that for any numbers $a$ and $b$ of $M$ the equality $(a*b)*a=b$ holds. Prove that there is a number $a$ such that $a*a=a$.

Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the sides $AC$, $AB$ and $BC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ $(AB=BC)$ so that $DE=DF$ and moreover the angles $\angle BAC$ and $\angle FDE$ are equal. Prove that $AE+FC=AC$.

Can non-zero digits be placed in the cells of a $10\times 10$ table so that all the $10$-digit numbers formed in the rows are greater than the $10$-digit number on the main diagonal, which in turn is greater than all the $10$-digit numbers in the columns of the table?
A square $ABCD$ is given in the plane. Find the minimum of the quotient $\dfrac{OA+OC}{OB+OD}$, where $O$ is an arbitrary point of the plane.
Prove that there exists a function $f(x)$ defined on $[0;+\infty)$ such that $f(f(\ldots(x)\ldots))=\frac{x}{x+1}$ (the function $f$ is applied $239$ times).

$1993$ points are marked on paper, and some of them are joined by non-intersecting segments so that no several of these segments form a closed broken line. Two players alternately put tokens on the marked points, and each next token must cover a point adjacent to the previous one (points are adjacent if they are joined by a segment). The player who cannot move loses. Prove that the first player can win.
The numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ lie in the interval $(-1;1)$. Prove the inequality $$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{1+a_ia_{i+1}}\geqslant\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{1+a_i^2}\qquad(a_{n+1}\equiv a_1).$$

The numbers $n-1$ zeros and one one are placed at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon. One may increase by $1$ all the numbers at the vertices of any regular $k$-gon inscribed in the given polygon. Can all the numbers be made equal by such operations?

There are $2p+1$ balls in two urns. Every second half of the balls from the urn containing an even number of balls is moved to the other urn. Let $k<2p+1$ be some natural number, and it is known that the numbers $p$ and $2p+1$ are prime. Prove that sooner or later one of the urns will contain exactly $k$ balls.

The joint-stock company "Yolki-palki" has $1994$ shareholders, and it is known that any $1000$ of them together own a controlling stake (that is, at least half of the shares). What is the largest share of the stock one shareholder can have?

Call a triangle "low" if at least two of its altitudes have length at most $1$. Four points are given in the plane such that all triangles formed by them are low. Prove that there exists a line from which all these points are at distance at most $1/2$.
Natural numbers $a_1$, $b_1$, $c_1$, $a_2$, $b_2$ and $c_2$ are such that $$a_1+a_2=31,\quad b_1+b_2=32,\quad c_1+c_2=1994.$$ Prove that the products $a_1b_1c_1$ and $a_2b_2c_2$ are not equal.

$1994$ volumes of an encyclopedia stand on a shelf. Every morning the librarian Fedya takes three volumes and rearranges them somehow in the same places, and every evening the cleaner Dusya swaps some two volumes. Prove that Dusya can act so that at any moment fewer than five volumes stand in their own places (initially the volumes are arranged by the cleaner).

Points $C_1$, $A_1$ and $B_1$ are taken on the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ of an arbitrary triangle $ABC$ respectively. Denote by $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ the areas of the triangles $AB_1C_1$, $BA_1C_1$ and $CA_1B_1$ respectively. Prove that $$\sqrt{S_1}+\sqrt{S_2}+\sqrt{S_3}\leqslant\frac32\sqrt{S_{\triangle ABC}}.$$

A square is divided into several rectangles so that every horizontal line meets exactly $n$ rectangles, and every vertical line exactly $m$ rectangles (only lines not containing sides of rectangles are considered). What is the smallest possible number of rectangles in the division?

Two players play a game. The first player has thought of a number, and the second player in a move may name any five distinct natural numbers not greater than $9$, after which the first player reports the sum of the thought number and one of the named digits. In what smallest number of moves can the second player guess the thought number?

At points $A$ and $B$ lying on different sides of an angle, perpendiculars to the sides are erected; they meet the bisector of the angle at points $C$ and $D$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $CD$ is equidistant from the points $A$ and $B$.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $n>1$ are such that $(a+b)^n$ is divisible by $ab$. Prove that $a^{n-1}$ is divisible by $b$.

The segments joining a point $P$ lying inside a square $ABCD$ with the vertices divide the square into four triangles. Prove that the ratio of the areas of some two of them lies in the interval $[3/5;\ 5/3]$.
The number $1994$ is written on the board. Every second its largest prime divisor is added to the number on the board. Prove that at some moment this number will be divisible by $1995$.
In a non-isosceles acute-angled triangle $ABC$ a point $O$ is taken such that $\angle OBC=\angle OCB=20^\circ$. Moreover, $\angle BAO+\angle OCA=70^\circ$. Find the angle $A$.

Pluses and minuses are placed in the cells of a $1995\times 1995$ table. One may choose $1995$ cells no two of which lie in the same row or the same column, and change the signs in the chosen cells. Prove that by such operations one can achieve that at most $1994$ pluses remain in the table.

All sequences of natural numbers $(a_n)$ of length $1994$ with the following property are considered: $a_1=1$, $a_{n+1}\leqslant 1+a_n$. Prove that the number of such sequences with an even sum of terms equals the number of sequences with an odd sum of terms.

$200$ tennis players hold a tournament according to the Shvambranian system. This means that every day before the next games they line up in non-increasing order of the points scored by that moment, and then split into $100$ pairs of players standing next to each other. Prove that if the tournament lasts long enough, then on some day the results of some two players will differ by more than $50$ points. (There are no draws in tennis; a player gets $1$ point for a win and $0$ for a loss.)
A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ has two real roots whose difference is not less than $1995$. Prove that the equation $$f(x)+f(x+1)+\ldots+f(x+1995)=0$$ has two real roots.
A point $O$ is chosen inside a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that $\angle OAD=\angle OCD$. Prove that $\angle OBC=\angle ODC$.

The chess piece "machine-gunner" attacks in one fixed direction vertically or horizontally (for example, horizontally to the left) any number of cells. What is the largest number of machine-gunners not attacking each other that can be placed on a $20\times 20$ chessboard?

Let $d(n)$ be the number of natural divisors of the number $n$. Can one choose one hundred natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$ so that for all $k$ from $1$ to $100$ the equality $$d(a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_k)=a_k$$ holds?

Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $\angle KCB=\angle LAB=\alpha$. The perpendiculars $BD$ and $BE$ are dropped from the point $B$ to the lines $AL$ and $CK$ respectively. The point $F$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. Find the angles of the triangle $DEF$.

A state has $2000$ cities. Some pairs of cities are connected by roads so that one can drive from any city to any other. Prove that this state can be divided into several republics (possibly just one) so that in each republic one can drive from any city to any other city of this republic in a unique way without leaving it. (Each republic must contain at least two cities.)

In a sequence $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ consisting of natural numbers, the sum of the first ten terms equals $100$, and starting from $a_{11}$ each number $a_n$ equals the number of indices $i<n$ such that $a_i+i\geqslant n$. It is known that $a_{11}=10$. Prove that from some place on all the terms of the sequence are equal to each other.
$p$ and $q$ are prime numbers such that $p^2+1$ is divisible by $q$, and $q^2-1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $p+q+1$ is a composite number.

Two intersecting circles are given in the plane. The point $A$ is one of the two intersection points of these circles. In each circle a diameter is drawn parallel to the tangent at the point $A$ to the other circle, and these diameters do not intersect. Prove that the endpoints of these diameters lie on one circle.

$1995$ points are given in the plane, and some pairs of points are joined by segments. The points are initially coloured in two colours. Every minute (simultaneously) those points that are joined to an even number of points of the same colour change their colour. Prove that the original colouring cannot be obtained again after an odd number of minutes.

$d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k$ are all the natural divisors of some natural number $N$, written in increasing order. It turned out that $$d_2-d_1,\ d_3-d_2,\ d_4-d_3,\ \ldots,\ d_k-d_{k-1}$$ are also all the divisors of some natural number (not necessarily in increasing order). Find all $N$ for which this is possible.

$1995$ shorties live in Flower Town. They have $995$ ten-kopeck coins and an unlimited supply of five-kopeck coins. Sometimes the shorties exchange coins: one gives another a $10$-kopeck coin, and the other gives him two five-kopeck coins. One evening each of the shorties declared: "Today I gave away exactly $10$ coins." Prove that one of them was mistaken.
Find all primes $p$ and $q$ for which $p^2-p+1=q^3$.

The numbers $0$, $1$, $\sqrt2$ are written on the board. One may add to any of these numbers the difference of the other two multiplied by an arbitrary rational number. Can the numbers $0$, $2$, $\sqrt2$ be obtained by such operations?
Find all natural $n$ for which $3^n+5^n$ is divisible by $3^{n-1}+5^{n-1}$.
$M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$, and $r_1$ and $r_2$ are the radii of the circles inscribed in the triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$. Prove that $r_1<2r_2$.

Several natural numbers are written on the board. One may erase two distinct numbers from the board and write instead their greatest common divisor and least common multiple. Prove that at some moment the numbers on the board will stop changing.

No three diagonals of a convex $1996$-gon pass through one point. Prove that the number of triangles whose vertices lie strictly inside this $1996$-gon and whose sides lie on its diagonals is divisible by $11$ (these are not necessarily triangles of the division; the triangles in question may be divided by diagonals into smaller parts).

Prove that for every polynomial $x^2+px+q$ with integer coefficients there is a polynomial $2x^2+rx+s$ with integer coefficients such that the sets of values of these polynomials at integer points do not intersect.
In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, $AB=BC$, $\angle ABE+\angle DBC=\angle EBD$ and $\angle AEB+\angle BDC=180^\circ$. Prove that the orthocentre of the triangle $BDE$ lies on the diagonal $AC$.

In a federal state consisting of two republics, every two cities are connected by a one-way road; moreover, moving along the roads, one can get from any city to any other. The travel agency "Hamilton" offers $n$ different tourist routes through the cities of the first republic and $m$ through the cities of the second (each of these routes visits every city of the republic exactly once and returns to the starting city, all without leaving the republic). Prove that the agency "Hamilton" could offer curious tourists at least $mn$ similar tourist routes through the cities of the whole federation.
Prove the inequality $$a^bb^a\leqslant\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{a+b}$$ for any positive numbers $a$ and $b$.

Segments $AE$ and $CF$ of equal length are laid off on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. The circle passing through the points $B$, $C$, $E$ and the circle passing through the points $A$, $B$, $F$ meet at points $B$ and $D$. Prove that the line $BD$ is the bisector of the angle $ABC$.

A sequence of natural numbers is defined by the relations $$a_1=1,\qquad a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{[\frac{n+1}{2}]}$$ ($[a]$ denotes the integer part of the number $a$). Prove that the last digits of the decimal representations of the numbers $a_n$ form a non-periodic sequence.

The building of Moscow University has very many lifts, and each lift carries passengers only between some two floors (but on each floor one can walk to any lift that stops there). It is known that from any floor one can get to any other using an even number of lifts and without passing through any floor twice. Prove that, if desired, the same can be done using an odd number of lifts.
The midpoints of the sides of a convex hexagon form a hexagon whose opposite sides are parallel. Prove that the long diagonals of the original hexagon pass through one point.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the set of collections $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{1996}$ of natural numbers satisfying the conditions $$a_1=1,\qquad a_{k+1}\leqslant a_k+1\quad(k=1, 2, \ldots, 1995);$$ let $\mathcal B$ be the set of collections $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^{1996}$ of natural numbers satisfying the conditions $$b_1=1,\qquad b_k\leqslant b_{k+1}\leqslant k+1\quad(k=1, 2, \ldots, 1995).$$ Prove that the sets $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ have equally many elements.
Denote by $S(n)$ the sum of all natural divisors of the number $n$ other than $n$. Prove that the equation $S(n)=1\,000\,000$ has fewer than $1\,500\,000$ solutions.

A domino lies on the squares $a1$ and $b1$ of a chessboard, and in addition a rook stands on the square $a1$. Two people play according to the following rules: the first moves the rook to some free square, after which the second places a domino covering this square and one more free square adjacent to it by a side. The player who cannot move loses, except in the case when the whole board is covered by dominoes; in this last case the first player wins. Who wins with correct play?

Trees of equal height grow on the equator of the planet Tranai. If they all fall to the west, the total length of the parts of the equator covered by more than five trees will be $100$ km. Prove that if all the trees fall to the east, the total length of the parts of the equator covered more than five times will also be $100$ km. (The height of the trees is much smaller than the size of the planet.)
Prove that there is no set of $100$ distinct natural numbers such that the sum of any $98$ of them is divisible by the sum of the remaining two.

The bisector of the angle $A$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meets the lines $BC$ and $CD$ at points $X$ and $Y$. The point $A'$ is symmetric to the point $A$ with respect to the line $BD$. Prove that the points $C$, $X$, $Y$ and $A'$ lie on one circle.

A warehouse holds $n$ different sacks and a watchman $(n>1)$. Each sack lies either on the floor of the warehouse or in one of the other sacks. From time to time the watchman chooses one of the sacks lying on the floor, takes out of it and puts on the floor all the sacks lying in it (without touching their contents), and at the same time puts into it all the other sacks lying on the floor (again together with their contents). Prove that there are exactly $n+1$ different arrangements of the sacks that the watchman can obtain by such operations. Two arrangements are considered the same if every sack has the same contents in the first of them as in the second.
A sequence of natural numbers $\{x_n\}$ is defined by the relations $$x_1=2,\qquad x_{n+1}=2x_n^2-1.$$ Prove that for all $n$ the numbers $x_n$ and $n$ are coprime.

Two parallel chords $AB$ and $CD$ are drawn in a circle $S$. The line drawn through $C$ and the midpoint of $AB$ meets $S$ a second time at a point $E$. The point $K$ is the midpoint of the segment $DE$. Prove that $\angle AKE=\angle BKE$.

The town of Neznakomsk has a million inhabitants, and any two of them have a common acquaintance among the others. Prove that one can choose $5000$ inhabitants of the town so that each of the others has at least one acquaintance among the chosen ones.
Natural numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy the equation $$2x^x+y^y=3z^z.$$ Prove that these numbers are equal.

A number $N$ is the product of $k$ distinct primes $(k\geqslant 3)$. Two players play the following game: they alternately write on the board composite divisors of the number $N$. The number $N$ itself may not be written; moreover, the appearance on the board of two coprime numbers or of two numbers one of which is divisible by the other is forbidden. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?

The points $K$, $L$, $M$, $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ respectively of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that the orthocentres of the triangles $AKN$, $BKL$, $CLM$, $DMN$ are the vertices of a parallelogram.

A $100\times 100$ grid square was folded several times along grid lines, and two straight cuts, also along grid lines, were made. Into what largest number of parts could the square have been cut in this way?

All faces of a convex polyhedron are triangles; at least $5$ edges issue from each vertex, and no two vertices from which exactly $5$ edges issue are joined by an edge. Prove that this polyhedron has a face from whose vertices respectively $5$, $6$ and $6$ edges issue.
$2n+1$ lines are placed in the plane. Prove that there are at most $n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$ different acute-angled triangles whose sides lie on these lines.
Prove that all twelve-digit numbers cannot be divided into groups of $4$ numbers so that in each group the numbers coincide in $11$ places and contain four consecutive digits in one place.

$360$ points divide a circle into equal arcs. $180$ non-intersecting chords with endpoints at these points are drawn. Consider $180$ more chords obtained from the given ones by rotating the circle through the angle $38^\circ$. Prove that the union of these $360$ chords cannot be a closed broken line.
The numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the equality $$\max(a,b)+\max(c,1997)=\min(a,c)+\min(b,1998).$$ Prove that $b\geqslant c$.

$O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The line $BO$ meets the circumscribed circle a second time at a point $D$, and the extension of the altitude dropped from the vertex $A$ meets the circle at a point $E$. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral $BECD$ equals the area of the triangle $ABC$.

A city lies on several islands connected by bridges. When travelling around the city, the inhabitants measure the length of their route by the number of bridges they have to cross. After one of the bridges was closed for repair, every citizen declared: "I have a friend to whom the shortest route now contains one bridge more than before." Prove that at least one of the islands is uninhabited.
Find all integer solutions of the equation $$p^2+q^2+pq=15r^2.$$

In the decimal expansion of an irreducible fraction $m/n$, every digit after the decimal point except the first is less than the sum of its two neighbouring digits by one and the same natural number $k$. Prove that $n\leqslant 819$.

$999$ non-intersecting segments with endpoints at the vertices of a regular $1998$-gon split these vertices into pairs. Prove that arrows can be placed on the segments so that the sum of the resulting vectors is zero.

The following may be done with a sequence of numbers $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$: choose an arbitrary index $k$, $1\leqslant k\leqslant n$, and replace the number $a_k$ in the sequence by $-(a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n)-k$. How many different sequences can be obtained by such transformations from the sequence $(0,0,\ldots,0)$?

$175$ passengers and two conductors ride in a trolleybus. Each passenger buys a ticket only after being asked to do so three times. First the first conductor asks one of the passengers who still have no ticket to buy one, then the second conductor does the same, and so on until everybody has bought a ticket. What is the largest number of ticket sales the first conductor can guarantee for himself?
Several powers of two are written on each of $10$ sheets of paper. The sums of the numbers on all the sheets are equal. Prove that some power of two occurs on these sheets at least $6$ times.

A country has $1998$ cities, and any two cities are connected by an airline. The ticket prices on all airlines are different. Can all circular routes (passing through every city exactly once and returning to the starting point) have the same cost?

Isosceles triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ are constructed on the segment $AC$ as the base, in different half-planes, with $\angle ADC=3\angle ACB$. $AE$ is a bisector of the triangle $ABC$, and the segments $DE$ and $AC$ meet at a point $F$. Prove that the triangle $CEF$ is isosceles.
Prove that for every natural $n>1$ one can choose three distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ between the numbers $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ such that $a^2+b^2$ is divisible by $c$.

Prove that the projections of the intersection point of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral onto two of its opposite sides are symmetric with respect to the line joining the midpoints of the other two opposite sides of this quadrilateral.

A set $M$ consists of $n$ points of the plane, no three of which lie on one line. For every triangle with vertices in $M$ the number of points of $M$ inside it was counted. Prove that the arithmetic mean of all the numbers found does not exceed $n/4$.

$999$ points are marked on a circle. In how many ways can the letters D, V and K be placed at these points so that on every arc between any two equal letters there is an even number of letters different from them?

A square $ABCD$ is divided into rectangles with equal perimeters whose sides are parallel to the sides of the square. It is known that the diagonal $AC$ meets all the rectangles. Prove that the diagonal $BD$ also meets all the rectangles.

$45$ languages are used on the island of New Babylonia, and every inhabitant knows at least five of them. It is known that any two inhabitants can talk to each other, possibly through several interpreters. Prove that then any two islanders can talk to each other using the services of at most $15$ interpreters.

A point $K$ is taken on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The bisector of the angle $CAK$ meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ a second time at a point $L$. Prove that if the line $LK$ is perpendicular to the segment $AB$, then either $AK=KB$ or $AK=AC$.

A natural number is written on the board. One may add to it any of its natural divisors (including one or the number itself) and write the result on the board instead of the original number. What is the smallest number of such operations that suffices to obtain a multiple of $683$ from any initial number? (Information: $683$ is a prime number.)

$AB$ is the shortest side of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the length of the broken line $AXYB$ is at least twice the length of $AB$.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are such that $$a^2+b^2+ab=c^2+d^2+cd.$$ Prove that the number $a+b+c+d$ is composite.

Several cells are cut out of a $1999\times 1999$ square of cells so that the remaining part can be divided into $1\times 2$ rectangles in a unique way. Prove that the number of cut-out cells is greater than $1000$.

A sequence $(x_n)$ of natural numbers is constructed by the following rule: $x_1=10^{1999}+1$, and for every $n\geqslant 2$ the number $x_n$ is obtained by deleting the first digit of the number $11x_{n-1}$. Is the set of terms of this sequence bounded?
The number $M$ is the product of all natural numbers from $1$ to $n$. Prove that every natural number less than $M$ can be represented as a sum of at most $n$ natural divisors of the number $M$.

For which $n\geqslant 3$ can the numbers from $1$ to $n$ be placed at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon so that the following property holds: for any three vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $AB=AC$, the number at the vertex $A$ is either greater than both numbers at the vertices $B$ and $C$ or less than both of them?

Points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ $(AB=BC)$. It is known that $\angle BC_1A_1=\angle CA_1B_1=\angle A$. $P$ is the intersection point of the segments $BB_1$ and $CC_1$. Prove that the quadrilateral $AB_1PC_1$ is cyclic.
How many $10$-digit numbers are there that are divisible by $66667$ and are written only with the digits $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$?

The numbers from $1$ to $100$ are placed in the cells of a $10\times 10$ table as follows: the bottom horizontal row contains the numbers from $1$ to $10$ in increasing order, the next row the numbers from $11$ to $20$ in increasing order, and so on. One may choose any three cells standing consecutively in a horizontal, vertical or diagonal row and either add $1$ to the numbers in the two end cells and subtract $2$ from the number in the middle cell, or, conversely, subtract $1$ in the two end cells and add $2$ in the middle one. After a series of such operations it turned out that the table again contains all the numbers from $1$ to $100$. Prove that their arrangement coincides with the original one.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $S$ with centre $O$. The bisector of the angle $ABD$ meets $AD$ and $S$ at points $K$ and $M$ respectively. The bisector of the angle $CBD$ meets $CD$ and $S$ at points $L$ and $N$ respectively. It is known that the lines $KL$ and $MN$ are parallel. Prove that the circumscribed circle of the triangle $MON$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $BD$.

A convex $n$-gon $(n>3)$ is divided into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals. Prove that one can mark $n-1$ segments among the drawn diagonals and the sides of the polygon so that no set of marked segments forms a closed broken line and no vertex is the endpoint of exactly two marked segments.

The sequences $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ and $y_1, y_2, \ldots$ are defined by the conditions $x_1=\frac18$, $y_1=\frac1{10}$, $x_{n+1}=x_n+x_n^2$, $y_{n+1}=y_n+y_n^2$. Prove that the numbers $x_m$ and $y_n$ are not equal for any natural $m$ and $n$.

$AA_1$ and $BB_1$ are altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The points $K$ and $M$ are the midpoints of the segments $AB$ and $A_1B_1$ respectively. The segments $AA_1$ and $KM$ meet at a point $L$. Prove that the points $A$, $K$, $L$ and $B_1$ lie on one circle.

$101$ lines are drawn in the coordinate plane, and all their points of intersection with each other are marked. Can it happen that on each of the drawn lines there lie $50$ marked points with positive first coordinates and $50$ with negative ones?
A number $N$ equals the product of $200$ distinct natural numbers. Prove that $N$ has at least $19901$ distinct natural divisors (including one and the number itself).

The cells of a $2000\times 2000$ square are painted according to the following rules. At any moment one may paint a single cell if none of its neighbouring cells has been painted yet; or a $1\times 2$ rectangle if exactly two of its neighbouring cells have already been painted by this moment; or a $2\times 2$ square if $8$ of its neighbouring cells have already been painted. (Cells sharing a side are considered neighbouring.) Can the whole square be painted?

One of the excircles of a triangle $ABC$ touches the side $AB$ and the extensions of the sides $CA$ and $CB$ at points $C_1$, $B_1$ and $A_1$ respectively. Another excircle touches the side $AC$ and the extensions of the sides $BA$ and $BC$ at points $B_2$, $C_2$ and $A_2$ respectively. The lines $A_1B_1$ and $A_2B_2$ meet at a point $P$, and the lines $A_1C_1$ and $A_2C_2$ at a point $Q$. Prove that the points $A$, $P$ and $Q$ lie on one line.

Call a natural number "almost prime" if it is not divisible by any prime number from the interval $[3,19]$. Call a number "very non-prime" if it has at least two prime divisors from the interval $[3,19]$. What is the largest number of almost prime numbers that can be chosen so that any two of them add up to a very non-prime number?

Several quadratic trinomials with leading coefficients equal to one and equal discriminants are given. The sum of any two of these trinomials has two roots. Prove that the sum of all the trinomials also has two roots.

$S_1$ and $S_2$ are two circles having no common points. A common (external) tangent touches them at points $A$ and $B$. A circle $S_3$ passes through $A$ and $B$ and meets $S_1$ and $S_2$ a second time at points $C$ and $D$ respectively. $K$ is the intersection point of the lines tangent to $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the points $C$ and $D$. Prove that $KC=KD$.
$a$ and $b$ are distinct natural numbers greater than $1$, and $a^2+b-1$ is divisible by $b^2+a-1$. Prove that the number $b^2+a-1$ has at least two distinct prime divisors.

$111$ non-overlapping three-cell corners lie on the plane of cells. They have the following property: for each of the corners, the $2\times 2$ square containing it is entirely covered by corners. Prove that one can remove one or several corners (but not all of them) so that this property is preserved.

There are $20$ distinct natural numbers whose set of pairwise sums (including the sums of each number with itself) contains exactly $201$ elements. What is the smallest number of elements the set of (positive) pairwise differences of these numbers can have?

$ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AD$ and $BC$. A circle touches the segments $AB$ and $AC$ and meets the segment $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$. The points $X$ and $Y$ are the intersection points, nearest to $D$, of the inscribed circle of the triangle $BCD$ with the lines $DM$ and $DN$ respectively. Prove that the line $XY$ is parallel to $AD$.

A positive number is written in every cell of a chessboard so that in every row the sum of the numbers equals $1$. It is known that for every placement of eight rooks not attacking each other on the board, the product of the numbers under them is not greater than the product of the numbers on the main diagonal. Prove that the sum of the numbers on the main diagonal is at least $1$.

Can one choose several points in space and join some pairs of points by segments so that exactly three segments issue from each point and every closed broken line made up of distinct segments has at least $30$ links?
Quadratic trinomials $f$ and $g$ with integer coefficients take only positive values, and $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\geqslant\sqrt2$ for all real $x$. Prove that $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}>\sqrt2$ for all real $x$.

The computer "Intel Pen'-V" can perform only one operation on a number: it adds $1$ to it, and then in the resulting number moves all the zeros to the end and rearranges the other digits arbitrarily (for example, from the number $1004$ it can obtain $1500$ or $5100$). The number $12345$ was entered into the computer, and after $400$ operations the screen showed the number $100000$. How many times during this period did a number ending in zero appear on the screen?

The point $O$ is the centre of the inscribed circle of a triangle $ABC$, and the point $D$ is the midpoint of the side $AB$. It is known that the angle $AOD$ is a right angle. Prove the equality $AB+BC=3AC$.
Rectangles $1\times 20$, $1\times 19$, $\ldots$, $1\times 1$ were cut out of a $20\times 20$ table. Prove that $36$ more $1\times 2$ rectangles can be cut out of the remaining part of the table.

A point $K$ is chosen on the bisector $AL$ of a triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle BKL=\angle KBL=30^\circ$. The lines $AB$ and $CK$ meet at a point $M$, and the lines $AC$ and $BK$ at a point $N$. Find the angle $AMN$.
Prove the inequality $$[m,n]+[m+1,n+1]>2m\sqrt n$$ for all natural numbers $n>m$, where $[x,y]$ is the least common multiple of the numbers $x$ and $y$.

In the parliament of the country of Alternativia, for any two deputies there is a third one who knows exactly one of them. Each deputy belongs to one of two ruling parties. Every day the president orders some group of deputies to move to the other party, and all deputies who know at least one of the deputies of the group also change their party affiliation. Prove that the president can achieve that all deputies of Alternativia without exception move to the party he himself supports. (The president is not a member of the parliament.)

Natural numbers not exceeding $10$ are written in a $10\times 10$ table. The numbers in any two cells adjacent by a side or a corner are coprime. Prove that some number occurs in the table at least $17$ times.

The bisectors of the angles $A$ and $B$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $P$, and the bisectors of the angles $C$ and $D$ at a point $Q$ different from $P$. The line $PQ$ passes through the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that $\angle ABC=\angle BAD$ or $\angle ABC+\angle BAD=180^\circ$.

Do there exist quadratic trinomials $f$ and $g$ with leading coefficients equal to one such that for every integer $n$ the number $f(n)g(n)$ is an integer, while the numbers $f(n)$, $g(n)$ and $f(n)+g(n)$ are not integers?

$10$ points numbered from $1$ to $10$ are marked in the plane. One may choose any rectangular coordinate system and write the numbers of the points in a row in increasing order of their first coordinates (provided that all first coordinates are distinct). What is the largest number of permutations of the numbers from $1$ to $10$ that can be obtained in this way from one set of points in the plane?

A natural number is written on the board. Two players move alternately, and each in his move replaces the number $n$ written on the board by the number $n-1$ or $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}\right]$ (square brackets denote the integer part). The player who first writes the number $1$ on the board wins. Who wins with correct play, the first player or his partner, if at the start of the game the number on the board is $1\,000\,000$?

The altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. A point $K$ is such that the circumscribed circles of the triangles $BHK$ and $CHK$ are tangent to the line $BC$. The point $D$ is the foot of the altitude dropped from the vertex $B$ to the side $AC$. Prove that the point $A$ is equidistant from the lines $KB$ and $KD$.
Let $n$, $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $n>1$. Prove that $(\sigma(n))^k\neq n^m$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of all natural divisors of the number $n$.

In a chess club visitors can play chess with each other or with a computer. Yesterday there were $n$ people in the club, each of them played at most $n$ games, and any two who did not play each other played at most $n$ games in total. Prove that at most $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ games were played in all.

Three quadratic trinomials with pairwise distinct leading coefficients are given. The graphs of any two of them have exactly one common point. Prove that all three graphs have exactly one common point.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given such that $\angle ABC=90^\circ$, $AC=CD$ and $\angle BCA=\angle ACD$. The point $F$ is the midpoint of the segment $AD$. The segments $BF$ and $AC$ meet at a point $L$. Prove that $BC=CL$.
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive numbers such that $a+x=b+y=c+z=1$. Prove the inequality $$(abc+xyz)\left(\frac1{ay}+\frac1{bz}+\frac1{cx}\right)\geqslant 3.$$

A $2002\times 100$ rectangle (the side of length $2002$ is horizontal) is divided into dominoes (i.e. $1\times 2$ rectangles) and four-cell skew pieces (a vertical skew piece in the source's picture: one cell in the upper row, two cells in the middle row, one cell in the bottom row, each row shifted by one cell). It is known that there are at most $600$ dominoes in this division. Prove that at least $800$ four-cell pieces in this division are placed horizontally (i.e. as a skew piece occupying two rows and three columns, in either of its two mirror forms).

The following operations may be performed on a number: $1^\circ$ raise it to any natural power; $2^\circ$ cut off its last two digits, multiply the number formed by them by $3$ and add the result to the number formed by the remaining digits. Can one obtain $82$ from the number $81$ by means of such operations?

Points $M$ and $N$ are chosen on the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ respectively such that $\frac{BN}{DN}=\frac{AM}{CM}$ and $\angle BAD=\angle BMC$. Prove that $\angle ANB=\angle ADC$.

A country has at least $100000$ cities, and exactly $2001$ roads issue from every city. Is it true that one can always close some of the roads (at least one, but not all) so that afterwards the same number of roads issues from every city?
A prime number $p>3$ is such that the equation $p^k+p^\ell+p^m=n^2$ has a solution in natural numbers. Prove that $p+1$ is divisible by $8$.
Prove that any $13$ numbers $$0=x_1\leqslant x_2\leqslant\ldots\leqslant x_{12}\leqslant x_{13}=1$$ can be divided into two groups whose arithmetic means differ by at least $\frac{13}{24}$.
problems.proposer: M. A. Lifshits, Yu. Lifshits, F. Petrov

problems.problem: An alchemist has $50$ substances. He can turn any $49$ substances, taken in equal shares, into the remaining substance without changing the total mass. Prove that he can achieve that he has equal amounts of all $50$ substances.

Points $X$ and $Y$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ respectively such that $XBYD$ is a parallelogram. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, and the lines $AC$ and $XY$ meet at a point $L$. Prove that the points $M$, $N$, $L$ and $D$ lie on one circle.
problems.proposer: D. Djukić, S. Berlov, D. Karpov, A. Pastor

problems.problem: $64$ vertices are given. Two players play the following game: in each move the first player joins by an edge two vertices not yet joined, and the second player orients this edge arbitrarily (i.e. introduces a direction of motion on it). The second player wins if after $1959$ moves the resulting graph is connected, and the first player wins otherwise. Who wins with correct play?## 6 | G | F. Petrov

The shore of a lake has the shape of a convex centrally symmetric $100$-gon $A_1A_2\ldots A_{100}$ with centre of symmetry $O$. Inside the lake there is an island $B_1B_2\ldots B_{100}$ such that $B_i$ is the midpoint of the segment $OA_i$ for all $i$ from $1$ to $100$. On the island there is a prison with a high fence along its edges. Two guards stand at opposite points of the shore. Prove that together they see the whole shore of the lake.

The secret code of any FBI safe is a natural number from $1$ to $1700$. Two spies each learned one code and decided to exchange this information. Having agreed on their actions in advance, they met on a river bank near a pile of $26$ stones. First the first spy threw several stones into the water, then the second, then the first again, and so on until the stones ran out. After that the spies parted. How could the information have been transmitted? (The spies did not say a single word to each other.)

A grasshopper jumps along the integer points of a line. Each of its jumps has length one. During each jump the grasshopper sings one of the $\frac{p-1}{2}$ songs he knows ($p$ is an odd prime number). Prove that the number of distinct musical routes of the grasshopper consisting of at most $p-1$ jumps and returning him at the end to the starting point is divisible by $p$.

Kostya was multiplying two $50$-digit numbers in a column. He wrote these numbers one under the other, then for each pair of digits in the same position computed their product and wrote the $50$ products obtained in a row without spaces in the corresponding order. Prove that the number obtained by Kostya is not equal to the product of the original $50$-digit numbers.

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given such that $\angle ABC+\angle ABD=90^\circ$. A point $E$ is marked on the diagonal $BD$ such that $BE=AD$. The perpendicular $EF$ is dropped from it to the side $AB$. Prove that $CD+EF<AC$.

An equilateral triangle with side $2003$ is drawn on a sheet of paper. Lines parallel to its sides divide it into $2003^2$ small equilateral triangles with side $1$. Fedya and Sasha move alternately. In each move a player traces with a felt-tip pen a closed broken line that runs along the sides of the unit triangles and is the boundary of a convex polygon. Different broken lines must have no common points. Fedya begins; the player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play?
problems.proposer: D. Karpov, A. Pastor (after a problem of F. Bakharev)

problems.problem: $n\geqslant 4$ natural numbers are given. It is known that the sum of the squares of any $n-2$ of these numbers is divisible by the product of the remaining two numbers. Prove that among these numbers there are at least two equal ones.

A country has $1000$ cities, and some pairs of cities are connected by roads. It turned out that one of the endpoints of every road is a city from which at most $10$ roads issue. What is the largest possible number of roads in this country?
problems.proposer: Several members of the jury led by S. Ivanov

problems.problem: A circle $\omega$ and a point $P$ outside it are given. A line $\ell$ passing through $P$ meets $\omega$ at points $A$ and $B$. A point $C$ is marked on the segment $AB$ such that $PA\cdot PB=PC^2$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the two arcs into which the chord $AB$ divides the circle $\omega$. Prove that the angle $\angle MCN$ does not depend on the choice of the line $\ell$.

A prime number $p$ and a natural number $n\geqslant p$ are given. Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$, $a_n$ be an arbitrary collection of natural numbers, and let $f_k$ be the number of $k$-element subsets of this collection whose sum is divisible by $p$. Prove that $\sum\limits_{k=0}^n(-1)^kf_k$ is divisible by $p$. (We assume that $f_0=1$.)

A quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^2+ax+b$ is given. A point $p$ is taken in the interval $(0,1)$ such that $p\neq-\frac a2$ and $f(b-f(p))>f(p)$. Prove that there is a point $q\neq p$ in the interval $(0,1)$ such that $f(p)=f(q)$.

A point $L$ is taken on the diagonal $AC$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ such that $AB=AL$. A point $F$ is taken on the ray $DC$ such that $DB=DF$. The point $E$ is symmetric to $B$ with respect to $AD$. Prove that the points $F$, $L$ and $E$ lie on one line.

Natural numbers $n$ and $d$ are such that $n!$ is divisible by $d$ and $d<n!$. Prove that there is a natural number $f$ such that $n!$ is divisible by $f$ and by $d+f$ ($n!=1\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot\ldots\cdot n$).
problems.proposer: A. Golovanov, A. Khrabrov, D. Rostovsky, S. Ivanov

problems.problem: A token stands at one of the vertices of a regular $4006$-gon. Two players play the following game: first the first player marks one of the vertices of the $4006$-gon. After that they alternately move the token according to the following rules: the token may be moved either along a main diagonal or along a shortest diagonal of the $4006$-gon (i.e. one joining two vertices that are separated by one vertex). It is forbidden to return the token to the vertex from which it has just come. Prove that the second player can always place the token on the vertex marked by the first player with one of his moves.

The point $K$ is the midpoint of the cevian $AD$ of a triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ on the segment $KC$ is such that $\angle ABK=\angle XBC$. It turned out that $S_{AKC}=S_{KBX}$. Prove that $\angle BAX=\angle BCX$.

A natural number is written on the board. The following operation may be performed on it: subtract $1$ from all its non-zero digits and then append at the end of the number the number of these ones. (For example, $11011321\rightarrow 2107$.) From which eight-digit numbers can the number $7$ be obtained by several such operations?

The edges of a graph are coloured in four colours so that in every path of three edges the first and the third edges have different colours (the beginning and the end of the path may coincide). Prove that the vertices of this graph can be coloured properly in four colours (i.e. so that any two vertices joined by an edge have different colours).
problems.proposer: S. Berlov, D. Karpov, A. Pastor

problems.problem: Find all pairs of natural numbers $a, b>1$ such that $a^b-1$ is divisible by $b^a$.
Several quadratic trinomials are given. Each of them has two roots, and the difference of any two of them has no roots. Prove that the sum of these trinomials has at least one root.
A $25$-digit number without nines in its decimal representation is given. Prove that one can increase two of its equal digits by $1$ so that the resulting number is not divisible by $7$.

Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $KB=LC$. The point $X$ is symmetric to $K$ with respect to the midpoint of the side $AC$, and the point $Y$ is symmetric to $L$ with respect to the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that the line containing the bisector of the angle $A$ bisects the segment $XY$.

$k$ cells are marked in a $100\times 100$ square so that for every cutting of the square into two rectangles along grid lines, one of the rectangles contains at least $100$ marked cells. For what smallest value of $k$ is this possible?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. A circle touches the side $AC$ at a point $B_1$ and the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $C_1$ and $A_1$ respectively. The circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB_1$ meets the line $A_1B_1$ a second time at a point $L$. Prove that the points $C_1$, $A$, $B_1$ and the midpoint of the segment $LA_1$ lie on one circle.

Two identical regular $111$-gons are cut out of cardboard. The vertices of each of them are numbered by the numbers from $1$ to $111$ in arbitrary order. Prove that they can be laid one on the other (possibly turning one over) so that no two vertices with the same number coincide.

A sequence of natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ is defined as follows: $a_1=1$, and for $n\geqslant 2$, $a_n$ is the smallest natural number that does not occur among the numbers $a_1$, $\ldots$, $a_{n-1}$ and is such that $a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n$ is divisible by $n$. Prove that $a_{a_n}=n$ for all $n$.
Some $10$ cells of a $10\times 10$ square are painted. For what largest $k$ is there certainly a grid rectangle of perimeter $k$ containing no painted cells?

Isosceles triangles $AFB$ and $BLC$ are constructed on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ as bases, one of them lying inside the triangle $ABC$ and the other constructed outwards. Moreover, $\angle AFB=\angle BLC$ and $\angle CAF=\angle ACL$. Prove that the line $FL$ cuts off an isosceles triangle from the angle $ABC$.
A sequence of positive numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ is defined by the equalities $a_1=2$ and $$a_{n+1}=\frac{n}{a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n}$$ for all natural $n$. Prove that $0.999<a_{2004}<1$.
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $a^3+b^3$ is divisible by $a^2+ab+b^2$, and the number $a-b$ is prime. Prove that $a^3-b^3$ is a perfect fourth power.

$100$ subsets are selected in an $N$-element set. All of them are even (i.e. consist of an even number of elements), all their possible intersections of $2$, of $3$, $\ldots$, of $99$ of them are also even, while the intersection of all $100$ subsets is odd. For what smallest $N$ is this possible?

$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral, and $K$ and $L$ are the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively. The line $KL$ meets the sides $AD$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. The circumscribed circle of the triangle $AKX$ meets the side $AB$ at a point $M$. Prove that the circumscribed circle of the triangle $BLY$ also passes through the point $M$.

A positive number not exceeding $1$ is written at every point of the plane. It is known that for every square with side $1$ the sums of the numbers at its opposite vertices are equal. Prove that all the numbers written in the plane are equal.
Natural numbers $a, b, c, d, e>1$ are such that $a^{b^{c^{d^e}}}=e^{d^{c^{b^a}}}$. Prove that $a=e$ and $b=d$.
Four quadratic trinomials are given. Their leading coefficients are equal to one, and the sum of any two of them has exactly one root. Prove that three of these four trinomials coincide.

A circle passing through the vertices $B$ and $C$ of a right triangle $ABC$ meets the hypotenuse $AC$ at a point $X$. The tangents to this circle drawn at the points $X$ and $B$ meet at a point $Y$. Prove that the point $Y$ lies on the midline of the triangle $ABC$ parallel to the side $BC$, or on its extension.

A lame king stands in the lower left corner of an $n\times n$ board; he can move only in three directions: to the right, up, and diagonally up-right. Denote by $A_n$ the number of all his routes leading to the opposite corner of the board, and by $A_n^*$ the number of such routes that do not enter the left column or the top row (except for the initial and final positions). Prove that $A_n^*=2A_{n-1}$.
Find all pairs of coprime natural numbers satisfying the equation $x^3-x=2(y^3-y)$.

Baron Munchausen shot $15$ ducks while hunting, weighing $50, 51, \ldots, 64$ kg. He knows the weight of each duck. Using a balance scale, the baron intends to prove to the spectators that the first duck weighs $50$ kg, the second $51$ kg, the third $52$ kg, and so on (initially the spectators know absolutely nothing about the weights of the ducks). What is the smallest number of weights the baron will need if both the weights and the ducks may be placed on both pans of the scale and the number of weighings is unlimited? (The weights of the weights are known both to the baron and to the spectators. An unlimited supply of weights of $1, 2, \ldots, 1000$ kg is available.)

$AE$ and $CD$ are altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The bisector of the angle $B$ meets the segment $DE$ at a point $F$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are taken on the segments $AE$ and $CD$ respectively such that the quadrilaterals $ADFQ$ and $CEFP$ are cyclic. Prove that $AP=CQ$.

$n$ distinct natural numbers are given. Their pairwise greatest common divisors and least common multiples were written on the board. What is the smallest possible number of distinct numbers written on the board?

Lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ touch a parabola at points $A$ and $B$ and meet at a point $C$. The point $K$ is the midpoint of the segment $AB$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $KC$ lies on the parabola.

In a company of one hundred people, among any ten there are three who are pairwise acquainted. Prove that one can choose eight of them so that each of the others is acquainted with someone among these eight.

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Moreover, the centre of the excircle of the triangle $XYC$ touching the side $XY$ lies on the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the segment $XY$ passes through the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$.
Prove that the equation $3^k=m^2+n^2+1$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.

Positive numbers $x_1$, $x_2$, $\ldots$, $x_n$ $(n\geqslant 2)$ are such that $$x_i\geqslant x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_{i-1}\quad\text{for } i=2, 3, \ldots, n.$$ Prove the inequality $$\frac{x_1}{x_2}+\frac{x_2}{x_3}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n-1}}{x_n}\leqslant\frac n2.$$

The numbers from $1$ to $n^2$ are written around a circle. One may swap two neighbouring numbers if these two numbers have not been swapped before. Prove that if at most $n^3/100$ such operations have been made, then one more can be made.

The altitudes $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. On the side $AC$ there is a point $L$ such that the segment $A_1L$ is bisected by the altitude $CC_1$, and the segment $C_1L$ is bisected by the altitude $AA_1$. Prove that $HL\perp OH$, where $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$.

A natural number $m$ divisible by $17$ is given. All possible sets of $17$ distinct natural numbers from $1$ to $m$ are considered, and for each such set the remainder of the sum of its numbers upon division by $m$ is computed. Prove that among the remainders obtained there are at least as many zeros as ones.

A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ and a number $a$ are given. It is known that the numbers $a$, $f(a)$, $f(f(a))$ and $f(f(f(a)))$ form a geometric progression with positive ratio. Prove that it is constant.
Points $K$, $L$ and $M$ are taken on the sides $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $\angle BAC=\angle KLM=\angle BCA$. Prove that if $AL+LM+MB>CL+LK+KB$, then $LM<LK$.

There are $100$ laths of lengths $1, 2, \ldots, 100$ cm. Two players play the following game: in a move one may choose three laths, form a triangle of them and burn it. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?
A prime number $p>2$ is given. Dima computed the remainders of the numbers $1!, 2!, 3!, \ldots, (p-1)!$ upon division by $p$. Prove that he obtained more than $\sqrt p$ distinct remainders.

The numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 11$ are written around a circle (in exactly this order). One may take a number, replace it by zero and add half of this number to each of its neighbours. Can eleven of these twelve numbers be made equal?

A triangle $ABC$ all of whose sides are different is given. Points $B_1$ and $B_2$ are marked on the rays $AB$ and $CB$ so that $AB_1=CB$, $CB_2=AB$. Points $A_1$ and $A_2$ are marked on the rays $CA$ and $BA$ so that $CA_1=BA$, $BA_2=CA$. Points $C_1$ and $C_2$ are marked on the rays $BC$ and $AC$ so that $BC_1=AC$, $AC_2=BC$. Prove that the lines $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$ and $C_1C_2$ meet at one point.

The numbers from $1$ to $2006$ are placed around a circle so that the following property holds: if $a+1$ is the left neighbour of the number $b$, then $b+1$ is the left neighbour of the number $a$ (it is assumed that $2006+1$ and $1$ are the same number). Prove that there is a number $x$ whose left neighbour is the number $x+1$.

$101$ natural numbers are given. It is known that the product of any $51$ of these numbers is divisible by the product of the remaining ones. Prove that if the numbers are coprime as a whole, then their product is the square of a natural number.

Let $I$ be the centre of the inscribed circle of a triangle $ABC$. A circle with centre at the point $I$ is drawn through the vertex $B$; it meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$, and meets the side $AC$ at two points $F$ and $L$ ($F$ lies between $A$ and $L$). Prove that the projections of the point $I$ onto $AC$, $BC$ and $BL$ lie on one line.

Positive numbers $x$, $y$, $z$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ satisfy the relations $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi$ and $$x^2+y^2+z^2=2(xy\cos\gamma+yz\cos\alpha+zx\cos\beta).$$ Prove that a triangle with angles $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ can be formed from segments of lengths $x$, $y$ and $z$.

A state has $100$ cities. Some pairs of cities are to be connected by flights so that one can fly from any city to any other and so that for any four cities $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ for which there are flights $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ there is also a flight $AD$. In how many ways can this be done?
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ satisfy the condition $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1$. Prove that $a+b+c+d+\frac1{abcd}\geqslant 18$.

Two young men in a snack bar treat a girl to sweets. In one move a young man buys $1$ or $2$ sweets from the barmaid and gives them to the girl. They move alternately. Initially each of the young men has $550$ roubles, and the barmaid has $1000$ sweets. Each sweet costs a rouble. The player who cannot treat the girl in his turn loses. Who wins with correct play?

Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ so that the segment $XY$ passes through the centre $I$ of the inscribed circle. The bisectors of the angles $AXY$ and $XYC$ meet on the side $AC$. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is obtuse.

Pairwise distinct numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$, $a_n$ and pairwise distinct numbers $b_1$, $b_2$, $\ldots$, $b_n$ belong to the interval $[0,1)$. The fractional parts of all pairwise sums $\{a_i+b_j\}$ for $1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n$ were written on the board. It turned out that at most $2n-2$ distinct numbers are written on the board. Prove that each number occurs on the board at least twice.
A quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^2+ax+b$ is such that the equation $f(f(x))=0$ has exactly one root. Prove that the coefficients $a$ and $b$ are non-negative.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ are drawn. The bisector of the exterior angle $C$ meets the lines $AB$ and $A_1B_1$ at points $L$ and $K$ respectively. It turned out that $CL=2CK$. Find the angle $C$ of the triangle.

Ten ones were written on the board. Every minute some $5$ numbers are increased by $50\%$, and the other $5$ numbers are decreased by $50\%$. Can it happen that after an hour the sum of the numbers on the board equals $10$?

A country has $100$ cities and $199$ roads. (Each road connects two cities, and any two cities are connected by at most one road.) One can drive along the roads from any city to any other. Prove that one can close several roads forming a closed route so that one can still drive along the remaining roads from any city to any other.

$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral such that $AD=BD=AC$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. The segment $MN$ meets the diagonals of the quadrilateral at points $X$ and $Y$, and $P$ is the intersection point of $AN$ and $DM$. Prove that $PX=PY$.

Fedya writes from left to right an infinite sequence of non-zero digits. After writing each digit he factors into primes the natural number obtained by that moment. Prove that sooner or later one of these prime factors will be greater than $100$.

$n^2$ distinct tokens stand on an $n\times n$ board. In one action one may arbitrarily rearrange the tokens standing in one row or in one column. Prove that in $3n-4$ actions one cannot obtain the arrangement symmetric to the original one with respect to the main diagonal.

In a group of $200$ people the following property holds: for any two people not acquainted with each other, each of the others is either acquainted with both of them or unacquainted with both of them. Prove that in this group one can find either $15$ pairwise acquainted or $15$ pairwise unacquainted people.
Distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the condition $$(a+b)(a+c)=(b+c)^2.$$ Prove that $$(b-c)^2>8(b+c).$$

The centre $I$ of the inscribed circle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ lies on the bisector of the acute angle between the altitudes $AA_1$ and $CC_1$. Prove that $IA_1=IC_1=IL$, where $L$ is the foot of the bisector of the angle $B$ of the triangle $ABC$.

To a natural number $a$ one may add any power of two by which the number $a+1$ is divisible. Prove that if one starts with some number and performs this operation every minute, then sooner or later a multiple of $2007$ will be obtained.

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $C$ and the orthocentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Points $Z$ and $T$ are chosen on the side $AC$ so that $ZX=ZY$ and $ZA=TC$. Prove that $BT\perp XY$.

$50$ points are marked in the plane, no three of which lie on one line. Kostya joins these points by segments having no common points with each other (including common endpoints). Kostya has already drawn $16$ segments. Prove that he can draw one more.
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ satisfy the relation $$(a^3+b^3)^4=c^3+d^3.$$ Prove the inequality $$a^4c+b^4d\geqslant cd.$$

An infinite collection of pairwise unequal rectangular parallelepipeds with integer sides is given. Prove that one of these parallelepipeds can be divided into several smaller ones, each of which is equal to one of the parallelepipeds of the collection.

A quadratic trinomial $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ is such that if any of its coefficients is replaced by $1$, a quadratic trinomial having at least one real root is obtained. Prove that the original trinomial takes a negative value at least at one point.
The point $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. It is known that $\angle AOC=\angle BAD=110^\circ$ and $\angle ABC>\angle ADC$. Prove that $AB+AD>CD$.
Distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given. Prove the inequality $$\gcd(ab+1,\ bc+1,\ ac+1)\leqslant\frac{a+b+c}{3}.$$

The host has thought of a number from $1$ to $n$. One may ask him several questions about this number at once, each to be answered "yes" or "no". Then the host answers all these questions, though not necessarily in the order in which they were asked. What is the smallest number of questions that must be asked in order to find out the host's number for certain?

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at a point $E$, and the segments $AC$ and $BD$ at a point $F$. Choose a point $P$ on the ray $EF$ such that $\angle BPE=\angle CPE$. Prove that $\angle APB=\angle DPC$.

A diagonal of a convex $100$-gon is called good if on each side of it there is an even number of sides. The $100$-gon was divided into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals, exactly $49$ of which are good. The triangles are coloured in two colours properly (i.e. triangles of the same colour cannot have a common side). Prove that there are equally many triangles of the first and of the second colour.
A sequence $(x_n)$ is defined as follows: $x_1=\frac12$ and $x_{n+1}=1-x_1x_2\cdots x_n$ for $n\geqslant 1$. Prove that $0.99<x_{100}<0.991$.

Monic quadratic trinomials $f_1$, $\ldots$, $f_{101}$ are given. All their pairwise sums have two roots each, and all these $101\cdot 100$ roots are distinct. Prove that the set of roots of the original trinomials cannot consist of exactly $98$ distinct numbers.
Let $p(a)$ be the smallest prime divisor of a natural number $a$. Natural numbers $m,n>1$ are such that $m^2+n=p(m)+p(n)^2$. Prove that $m=n$.

Elections took place in Wonderland. At each of $30$ polling stations $1000$ voters were registered. It is known that at each station the share of votes for the party "VEDRO" was greater than zero and equal to the share of the voters of this station who came to the elections. According to the official data, the party "VEDRO" received exactly $64.3\%$ of the votes of the number of voters who came to the elections. Prove that the official data are wrong.

Let $I$ and $I_A$ be respectively the centres of the inscribed circle and the excircle of a triangle $ABC$. The line $\ell_A$ passes through the orthocentres of the triangles $BIC$ and $BI_AC$. The lines $\ell_B$ and $\ell_C$ are defined similarly. Prove that the lines $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$ and $\ell_C$ meet at one point.

There are $140$ matches in a pile. Two players alternately take matches, the first from $1$ to $3$, the second from $1$ to $5$. When all the matches have been taken, the difference between the numbers of matches of the players is computed. If it is divisible by $7$ or by $13$, the second player wins; otherwise the first player wins. Who wins with correct play?

A parallelogram $ABCD$ is given such that $\angle BAC=40^\circ$ and $\angle BCA=20^\circ$. Points $E$ and $G$ are marked on the diagonal $AC$, and points $F$ and $H$ on the side $AD$, so that the points $B$, $E$ and $F$ lie on one line, $\angle ABG=\angle AHG=90^\circ$, and $AF=EG$. Prove that $AF=HD$.
A polynomial of degree $n$ (where $n$ is not divisible by $2$) with rational coefficients has exactly $n$ real roots forming a geometric progression. Prove that at least one of its roots is rational.

Call the distance between two vertices of a graph the length of the shortest path between them (the length of a path is measured in edges). A graph has $n>7$ vertices and at least $\frac{n(n-7)}{2}+10$ edges. Prove that the vertices of our graph can be divided into two groups so that the distance between any two vertices from different groups is not equal to three edges.
Natural numbers $x$ and $y$ are such that $\gcd(x^7,y^4)\cdot\gcd(x^8,y^5)=xy$. Prove that $xy$ is a perfect cube.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the equality $AB=CD$ holds. Its diagonals meet at a point $O$. The points $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and $T$ are the midpoints of the segments $BC$, $AD$, $AC$ and $BD$ respectively. Prove that the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $OZT$ lies on the line $XY$.

The quadratic trinomials $f(x)$, $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ have discriminants equal to $2$, and the quadratic trinomials $f(x)+g(x)$, $g(x)+h(x)$ and $f(x)+h(x)$ have discriminants equal to $1$. Prove that the quadratic trinomial $f(x)+g(x)+h(x)$ has no roots.

The streets of Moscow consist of several concentric circles (ring roads) and several radial avenues drawn from the centre $O$ to the outermost ring. The crossroads $A$ and $B$ lie on the outer ring. Three friends are going to drive from $A$ to $B$: Dima along the outer ring; Kostya first along the avenue $AO$ and then along the avenue $OB$; while Sergei claims that he knows a path shorter than both of the previous ones. Prove that he is wrong.

Call a board an arbitrary set of cells of the grid plane. A set of rooks on a board is called beautiful if they do not attack each other but attack all the other cells of the board. (A rook attacks every cell lying in the same row or the same column as it, even if not all cells between them belong to the board.) Prove that if on some board one can place a beautiful set of $2008$ rooks and one can place a beautiful set of $2010$ rooks, then one can also place a beautiful set of $2009$ rooks.
problems.proposer: K. Kokhas, S. Berlov, F. Petrov et al.

problems.problem: A sequence $x_n$ is given such that $x_{n+2}=|x_{n+1}|-x_n$. Prove that it is periodic.

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $C$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets its sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $Y$ and $X$ respectively. The segments $AX$ and $CY$ meet at a point $O$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the segments $AC$ and $XY$. Prove that the line $BO$ is tangent to the circumscribed circle of the triangle $MON$.
A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ is given. Is it always possible to find a polynomial $g(x)$ of degree four such that the equation $f(g(x))=0$ has no solutions?

For each of ten consecutive thirty-digit numbers, its largest divisor less than the number itself was written on the board. Prove that among the numbers written there are two ending in the same digit.

The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $AD$ and $BC$ so that $XD=3AX$ and $YC=3BY$. It turned out that $\angle MXA=\angle MYB=90^\circ$. Prove that $\angle XMN=\angle ABC$.

A country has $2010$ cities, from each of which exactly three roads lead to other cities. The president and the prime minister play the following game: they alternately sell roads to three private companies (initially all roads belong to the state; in each move a player sells exactly one road). The prime minister moves first. The president wants to achieve that for at least one city all three roads issuing from it are sold to different companies, and the prime minister wants to prevent this. The loser resigns. Which of the two politicians can keep his post with correct play?

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ $(AB=BC)$ the midpoints $X$ and $Y$ of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively are marked. The point $Z$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the point $B$ to the line $CX$. Prove that the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $XYZ$ lies on the line $AC$.

A natural number is given. The largest prime number not exceeding it is subtracted from it. The same operation is performed on the result again, and so on. Prove that there exists a number from which zero is obtained for the first time after exactly $1000$ steps.

Initially a $200\times 200$ square is coloured black and white in a chessboard pattern. One may choose any $2\times 3$ grid rectangle lying in our square and recolour each of its cells into the opposite colour. Can all cells be made the same colour by several such operations?

The teacher gave each pupil of class 10"A" a quadratic trinomial, then wrote $4$ numbers on the board and told each pupil to substitute these four numbers into his quadratic trinomial. Vasya obtained the values $2$, $3$, $5$ and $8$. Petya managed to substitute only the first three numbers and obtained $16$, $15$ and $13$, and when he was about to substitute the fourth number, it turned out that the teacher had already erased the task from the board. Help Petya find the fourth value (the answer must be justified, otherwise Petya will decide that he is being mocked).

For every natural number from $n+1$ to $n+1000$, all its divisors not exceeding $1000$ are written out. Prove that for infinitely many natural $n$ the sum of all the numbers written out is greater than a million, and for infinitely many it is less.

The point $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with angle $\angle B=30^\circ$. The ray $BO$ meets $AC$ at a point $K$. The point $L$ is the midpoint of the arc $OC$ of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $KOC$ not containing the point $K$. Prove that $A$, $B$, $L$, $K$ lie on one circle.

The town of Ugryumov has $2\,000\,000$ inhabitants who communicate little with each other. Nevertheless, among any $2000$ inhabitants there are three pairwise acquainted. Prove that the town has four inhabitants pairwise acquainted with each other.

Call a number $x$ far from squares and cubes if for every integer $k$ the inequalities $|x-k^2|>10^6$ and $|x-k^3|>10^6$ hold. Prove that there exist infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the number $2^n$ is far from squares and cubes.

There is a garland of $n$ light bulbs. Initially some of them are switched on and some are not. One may take any lit bulb (only a lit one!) and switch it off, changing at the same time the state of the two neighbouring bulbs (switching lit ones off and unlit ones on). For which $n$ can all the bulbs be switched off by these operations regardless of their initial state?

On the diagonal $AC$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ there is a point $P$ lying inside the triangle $ABD$ for which $$\angle ACD+\angle BDP=\angle ACB+\angle DBP=90^\circ-\angle BAD.$$ Prove that either $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=90^\circ$ or $\angle BDA+\angle CAB=90^\circ$.
Prove that the system of equations $$\begin{cases}x^3-ax^2+b^3=0\\ x^3-bx^2+c^3=0\\ x^3-cx^2+a^3=0\end{cases}$$ has no real solutions if the numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are distinct.

Points $C$ and $D$ are chosen on the side $BE$ of a triangle $ABE$ so that $BC=CD=DE$. The points $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and $T$ are the centres of the circumscribed circles of the triangles $ABE$, $ABC$, $ADE$ and $ACD$ respectively. Prove that $T$ is the intersection point of the medians of the triangle $XYZ$.

$25$ schoolchildren take part in the Unified State Exam. The exam consists of several questions, to each of which one of five answer options can be given. It turned out that any two schoolchildren answered at most one question in the same way. Prove that the exam had at most $6$ questions.

Several non-zero real numbers are placed around a circle. For any two numbers $a$ and $b$ standing next to each other, the numbers $a+b$ and $\frac1a+\frac1b$ are integers. Prove that among the given numbers there are at most four distinct ones.

A natural number has exactly a million natural divisors (including one and the number itself). They are written out in decreasing order. What is the smallest possible number of divisors that the $250$-th number in this list can have?

$ABCD$ is a parallelogram, and the line $\ell$ passes through $B$ perpendicular to $BC$. Two circles with common chord $CD$ touch the line $\ell$ at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that the segments $DP$ and $DQ$ are seen from the midpoint of $AB$ at equal angles.

In the coordinate plane, $100$ non-intersecting unit segments parallel to the coordinate axes are drawn in the first quadrant. These segments are mirrors (on both sides); they reflect light according to the rule "the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection". (When it hits the end of a mirror, a ray of light does not change its direction.) From a point lying in the unit disc with centre at the origin, a ray of light is emitted in the direction of the bisector of the first coordinate angle. Prove that this initial point can be chosen so that the ray is reflected from the mirrors at most $150$ times.

A natural number $A$ is called interesting if it is divisible by every number that remains after deleting several last digits of $A$. Find the largest interesting number consisting of distinct digits.

Call a quadrilateral equidiagonal if its diagonals are equal. The segment joining the midpoints of two opposite sides of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ divides it into two equidiagonal quadrilaterals. Prove that the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is itself equidiagonal.

Black and white points stand around a circle (at least $12$ of them), so that for each point, among its $10$ neighbours ($5$ on the left and $5$ on the right) there are equally many black and white ones. Prove that the number of points is divisible by $4$.

$100$ numbers from the interval $(0,1)$ are written on the board. One may choose two numbers $a$ and $b$ and replace them by the two roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2-ax+b$ (if this trinomial has two roots). Prove that this process cannot continue indefinitely.

The diagonals of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $O$. The points $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric to the point $O$ with respect to the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AD$ respectively. It is known that $AB=BC=CD$. Prove that the intersection point of the perpendicular bisectors of the diagonals of the quadrilateral lies on the line $XY$.

There are $85$ soldiers in a company.
